Dear
deer
a. (costly, precious, held at high value; used of Christ the Son, of the saints, and of a life a man may or may not count precious to himself)
Old English deore, precious or costly — the same root as dearth, since what is scarce is dear. The Greek is agapetos, beloved, the verbal adjective of agapao; the Hebrew is yaqqir, precious or costly.

Biblical Definition

Dear in the Authorized Version keeps its old commercial edge: a thing is dear when it costs much. So the Father's love for the Son is set out in the language of price — “Who hath delivered us from the power of darkness, and hath translated us into the kingdom of his dear Son” (Colossians 1:13). The kingdom into which the elect are translated is the kingdom of the Son whom the Father holds most precious, and that is the measure of the mercy. The same word describes the standing of the redeemed: “Be ye therefore followers of God, as dear children” (Ephesians 5:1). Adoption is not bare legal transfer; the adopted are held dear, and the imitation commanded flows from that settled affection rather than from an attempt to earn it. The LORD uses the word of an apostate people He will not finally cast off: “Is Ephraim my dear son? is he a pleasant child?” (Jeremiah 31:20). And Paul turns the word against himself, weighing his own life on the same scale and finding it light: “neither count I my life dear unto myself, so that I might finish my course with joy” (Acts 20:24). What is dear to God orders what may be counted dear by us.

Webster 1828 Definition

Webster (1828) defines dear first as of a high price, then as beloved and precious — both senses live in the Authorized Version.

expand to see more

DEAR, a. Scarce; not plentiful; as a dear year.

2. Bearing a high price in comparison of the usual price; more costly than usual.

3. Of a high value in estimation; greatly beloved; precious.

4. Beloved; as a dear friend.

DEARTH, n. Scarcity; such a want of any thing as renders it dear.

Key Scripture

Colossians 1:13 — "Who hath delivered us from the power of darkness, and hath translated us into the kingdom of his dear Son:"

Ephesians 5:1 — "Be ye therefore followers of God, as dear children;"

Jeremiah 31:20 — "Is Ephraim my dear son? is he a pleasant child? for since I spake against him, I do earnestly remember him still: therefore my bowels are troubled for him; I will surely have mercy upon him, saith the LORD."

Acts 20:24 — "But none of these things move me, neither count I my life dear unto myself, so that I might finish my course with joy, and the ministry, which I have received of the Lord Jesus, to testify the gospel of the grace of God."

Modern Corruption

Dear has decayed into a formality at the head of a letter, and the costly weight the word carried in 1611 is gone.

expand to see more

Nothing so drains a word as making it compulsory. Dear Sir at the head of a bill means nothing whatever, and the word has been worn smooth by the salutation until English readers pass over Colossians 1:13 without hearing it. The Authorized translators chose dear because it said costly. The kingdom of His dear Son is the kingdom of the Son whom the Father prizes above all, and the deliverance of sinners into that kingdom is measured by exactly that price. Where the word is heard as a politeness, the doctrine is heard as a pleasantry.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition; the loss is one of ordinary erosion rather than deliberate assault. The principle to recover is the old economy of the word. Nothing is dear that costs nothing. Adoption is dear because the Son was given; the church is dear because it was purchased with His own blood; and a man's own life, weighed against a course to be finished, is not dear at all. Paul's arithmetic in Acts 20:24 is only shocking to those who have forgotten what the word means.

Greek & Hebrew Roots

Greek agapetos, beloved — Colossians 1:13, Ephesians 5:1; timios, precious or costly — Acts 20:24; Hebrew yaqqir, precious — Jeremiah 31:20.

expand to see more

Greek agapetos — beloved, the verbal adjective of agapao; rendered dear at Colossians 1:13 and Ephesians 5:1.

Greek timios — held at a price, precious; Acts 20:24, where Paul declines to price his own life highly.

Hebrew yaqqir — costly, precious, rare; Jeremiah 31:20 of Ephraim, and of precious stones elsewhere.

Old English deore — costly; the same root as dearth, scarcity being what makes a thing dear.

The commercial sense governs the theological one: what God holds dear He has paid for.

Usage

"“The kingdom of his dear Son” — the price of the kingdom stated in one adjective."

"“As dear children” — the ground of imitation is settled affection, not probation."

"“Neither count I my life dear unto myself” — Paul's valuation of his own life over against his course."
